title: Client–server basics and how systems scale
summary: How a request flows from client to server, vertical vs horizontal scaling, stateless services, and why statelessness is what lets you add machines.
note:
1. Request path
   • Client → DNS → load balancer → app server → database
2. Scale up vs out
   • Vertical = bigger box (simple, capped, single point)
   • Horizontal = more boxes (needs LB + stateless app)
3. Stateless wins
   • Keep session/user state out of the app server (JWT, Redis, DB)
   • Any box can serve any request → add/remove freely
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: Vertical vs horizontal scaling in one line each?
recall.a: Vertical = a bigger single machine; horizontal = more machines behind a load balancer.

recall.q: Why must app servers be stateless to scale out?
recall.a: So any server can handle any request; no request is tied to one box's in-memory session.

recall.q: Where does per-user session state live in a stateless design?
recall.a: In the client token (JWT) or a shared store like Redis/DB, not in app-server memory.

shot.title: Scaling at a glance
shot.body:
| | Vertical (scale up) | Horizontal (scale out) |
|---|---|---|
| how | bigger CPU/RAM | more machines |
| ceiling | hardware limit | ~none |
| failure | single point | survives node loss |
| needs | nothing extra | LB + stateless app |

sections.title: How a request flows
sections.body:
✍️ A typical read: browser resolves the host via **DNS**, hits a **load balancer**, which forwards to one **app server**; the app talks to a **database** or **cache** and returns a response.
✍️ Each hop is a place to add capacity or fail — this is the map you reason over in a design interview.

sections.title: Scale up vs scale out
sections.body:
✍️ **Vertical (up):** give one machine more CPU/RAM. Easy, no code changes, but has a hardware ceiling and remains a single point of failure.
✍️ **Horizontal (out):** run many machines behind a load balancer. Near-unlimited and fault-tolerant, but requires the app to be stateless and introduces coordination concerns (shared data, caching).

sections.title: Stateless services
Where the bottleneck moves
sections.body: ✍️ Once app servers are stateless and horizontally scaled, the **database** usually becomes the bottleneck. The next moves are caching (read load), replication (read scaling), and sharding (write/storage scaling) — covered in later pages.
